DataComR for PROC COMPARE users

Source: vignettes/DataComR.Rmd
DataComR.Rmd

DataComR compares a Base dataset with a Compare dataset the way SAS PROC COMPARE does. If you know PROC COMPARE, you already know most of DataComR: the same concepts, the same comparison rules, a Listing laid out like the SAS one, and a Return code with the same bits as SYSINFO.

library(DataComR)

A first comparison

In SAS you would write:

proc compare base=base compare=compare;
  id subject visit;
run;

In R:

base <- data.frame(
  subject = c("A", "A", "B", "C"),
  visit = c(1, 2, 1, 1),
  weight = c(70.5, 71, 82, 64.2),
  group = c("x", "x", "y", "z")
)
compare <- data.frame(
  subject = c("A", "A", "B", "D"),
  visit = c(1, 2, 1, 1),
  weight = c(70.5, 71.5, 82, 58),
  group = c("x", "x", "w", "z")
)

comparison <- df_compare(base, compare, id = c("subject", "visit"))
comparison
#> ── The COMPARE Procedure ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Comparison of Base with Compare
#> (Method=EXACT)
#> 
#> Data Set Summary
#>

#>   Number of Observations in Common: 3.
#>   Number of Observations in Base but not in Compare: 1.
#>   Number of Observations in Compare but not in Base: 1.

#>   Total Number of Observations Read from Compare: 4.
#>

#>   Number of Observations with All Compared Variables Equal: 1.

#>   Number of Variables Compared with Some Observations Unequal: 2.
#>   Total Number of Values which Compare Unequal: 2.
#>   Maximum Difference: 0.5.
#> 
#> Variables with Unequal Values
#> 
#>     Variable  Type       Ndif  MaxDif
#>     weight    numeric       1     0.5
#>     group     character     1
#> 
#> Value Comparison Results for Variables
#> 
#>   ____________________________________________________________________
#>                         ||       Base    Compare
#>   subject    visit      ||     weight     weight      Diff.     % Diff
#>   _________  _________  ||  _________  _________  _________  _________

Printing the result gives the Listing. The same information is available as data:

differences(comparison)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 7
#>   subject visit variable base  compare  diff pct_diff
#>   <chr>   <dbl> <chr>    <chr> <chr>   <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1 A           2 weight   71    71.5      0.5    0.704
#> 2 B           1 group    y     w        NA     NA
unmatched_rows(comparison)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 3
#>   subject visit dataset
#>   <chr>   <dbl> <chr>  
#> 1 C           1 Base   
#> 2 D           1 Compare
return_code(comparison)
#> [1] 4288

differences() has one row per Unequal value. base and compare are character, so values of every type fit in one table, and numbers are shown at full precision: two values that compare unequal never look the same. For numeric variables, diff is Compare minus Base and pct_diff is diff as a percentage of the Base value.

From PROC COMPARE to df_compare()

PROC COMPARE DataComR
BASE= base
COMPARE= compare
ID statement id
no ID statement (by position) id = NULL (data frames only)
VAR statement var
WITH statement with
METHOD= method: "exact", "absolute", "relative", "percent"
METHOD=RELATIVE(δ) method = "relative", relative_delta = δ
CRITERION= criterion (default 1e-5)
MAXPRINT= max_print (default 50, per variable)
the Listing print()
OUT= differences differences()
&SYSINFO return_code()

The Return code

return_code() returns an integer whose bits flag each kind of difference, with the same values as SAS’s SYSINFO, so checks written for SAS carry over. 0 means the datasets are fully equal.

Bit Meaning
1 Dataset labels differ
8 Variable formats differ
16 Variable widths differ
32 Variable labels differ
64 Base has observations not in Compare
128 Compare has observations not in Base
1024 Base has variables not in Compare
2048 Compare has variables not in Base
4096 A value compares unequal
8192 Conflicting types
65536 Duplicate IDs (DataComR only)

SAS bits that have no meaning in R (dataset type, informat, BY groups) are never set. Test a single condition with bitwAnd():

bitwAnd(return_code(comparison), 4096) > 0
#> [1] TRUE

Matching observations

With id, observations are paired on their ID values; neither dataset needs to be sorted first. Without id, observations are paired by position, as SAS does without an ID statement, and results identify observations by an obs column:

differences(df_compare(base, compare))
#> # A tibble: 4 × 6
#>     obs variable base  compare  diff pct_diff
#>   <int> <chr>    <chr> <chr>   <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1     4 subject  C     D        NA     NA    
#> 2     2 weight   71    71.5      0.5    0.704
#> 3     4 weight   64.2  58       -6.2   -9.66 
#> 4     3 group    y     w        NA     NA

An ID value shared by more than one observation in a dataset is a Duplicate ID. SAS pairs duplicates in the order they appear; DataComR warns, lists them in the Listing, sets bit 65536, and leaves them out of the comparison, so they are never paired arbitrarily.

Comparing values

Comparison methods

method and criterion follow SAS’s formulas, with b the Base value and c the Compare value:

  • "exact" (the default): b == c
  • "absolute": |b - c| <= criterion
  • "relative": |b - c| / ((|b| + |c|) / 2 + relative_delta) <= criterion
  • "percent": 100 * |b - c| / |b| <= criterion

They apply to numeric variables only. A value computed in R, such as 0.1 + 0.2, fails the exact comparison against a stored 0.3; a small criterion accepts it:

b <- data.frame(id = 1, x = 0.1 + 0.2)
c <- data.frame(id = 1, x = 0.3)
return_code(df_compare(b, c, id = "id"))
#> [1] 4096
return_code(df_compare(b, c, id = "id", method = "absolute", criterion = 1e-9))
#> [1] 0

Type families

SAS has numeric and character variables; R has many more types. DataComR groups them into SAS-like Type families:

  • numeric: integer, double and logical, so 1L equals 1;
  • character: character and factor, compared by their labels;
  • date: compared exactly, never with a criterion;
  • datetime: compared as instants, so the same moment in two time zones is equal.

A type difference within a family (integer against double) is listed in the Listing but sets no bit. Variables from different families have Conflicting types: they are listed, set bit 8192, and their values are not compared.

Missing values and blanks

  • Missing equals missing; NaN counts as missing.
  • Special missings (haven’s tagged NAs, SAS’s .A to .Z) are equal only when they carry the same letter.
  • A missing value against a non-missing value is unequal.
  • Trailing blanks are ignored in character values, as SAS pads them; set ignore_trailing_blanks = FALSE to compare them. Leading blanks always count.

Choosing variables

var restricts which variables have their values compared; with pairs each var variable with a differently named Compare variable:

renamed <- compare
names(renamed)[names(renamed) == "weight"] <- "wt"
differences(df_compare(
  base, renamed,
  id = c("subject", "visit"), var = "weight", with = "wt"
))
#> # A tibble: 1 × 7
#>   subject visit variable base  compare  diff pct_diff
#>   <chr>   <dbl> <chr>    <chr> <chr>   <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1 A           2 weight   71    71.5      0.5    0.704

As in SAS, var limits only the value comparison: variables found in only one dataset, Conflicting types and Attribute differences are still reported.

Labels, formats and widths

Like PROC COMPARE, DataComR compares metadata as well as values. The label, format.sas and width attributes that haven sets when it reads SAS files, and the dataset label, are compared and reported as Attribute differences. They set their own Return code bits and never count as Unequal values.

labelled <- base
attr(labelled$weight, "label") <- "Weight (kg)"
attr(labelled$weight, "format.sas") <- "8.1"
relabelled <- base
attr(relabelled$weight, "label") <- "Body weight"
attr(relabelled$weight, "format.sas") <- "8.1"

return_code(df_compare(labelled, relabelled, id = c("subject", "visit")))
#> [1] 32

Large data: arrow and duckdb

base and compare can also be arrow Tables or Datasets, or duckdb tables, in any combination with data frames. The comparison then runs inside arrow or duckdb, and only counts and Unequal values are brought into R, so datasets larger than memory can be compared:

con <- DBI::dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb())
#> duckdb keeps downloaded extensions and secrets in a temporary directory:
#> ℹ /tmp/Rtmpi9028t/duckdb
#> This is removed when the R session ends.
#> • Extensions are re-downloaded each session.
#> • Secrets are lost.
#> ℹ Run duckdb(shared_home = TRUE) (or create ~/.duckdb) to keep them (suitable for most users).
#> ℹ Run duckdb(shared_home = FALSE) to accept the temporary directory (and silence this message).
#> ℹ See ?duckdb_storage for details and alternatives.
base_db <- dplyr::copy_to(con, base, "base")

differences(df_compare(base_db, compare, id = c("subject", "visit")))
#> # A tibble: 2 × 7
#>   subject visit variable base  compare  diff pct_diff
#>   <chr>   <dbl> <chr>    <chr> <chr>   <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1 A           2 weight   71    71.5      0.5    0.704
#> 2 B           1 group    y     w        NA     NA

DBI::dbDisconnect(con, shutdown = TRUE)

arrow and duckdb are optional; install them only if you need them. Matching by position needs data frames, because the order of rows in arrow and duckdb isn’t guaranteed, and duckdb tables carry no R attributes, so no Attribute differences are reported for them.

Where DataComR differs from PROC COMPARE

  • Variable names are case-sensitive, as R’s are: USUBJID and usubjid are different variables. Set ignore_case = TRUE to match names regardless of case, as SAS does.
  • Duplicate IDs are not paired (see above), and set their own bit.
  • A negative criterion is an error; SAS reads it as a multiple of machine precision.
  • Mismatched var and with (different lengths, or a var variable missing from the Compare dataset) are errors rather than warnings.
  • Not supported: BY groups, comparing variables within a single dataset, and OUT=/OUTSTATS= datasets (use differences() instead).
